name: Vera Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a new estate of affordable houses out past the ring road, for a timber-frame builder called Larchfield Homes. The wall panels come off a lorry already made in a factory, insulation and all, and we stand them up, fix them together, put the floor joists in and batten out for the plasterers. I'm the improver, which means I do what I'm told and I'm still learning, at fifty-eight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cooked in a care home for twenty-three years, and when it changed hands and the new lot cut the kitchen staff, I thought, right, Vera, now or never. The council and the union ran a scheme to get women into the trades, so I did a course and Bernie, the site foreman, took a chance on me. I'm the only woman on site most days and I've got the oldest knees.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the morning when a house goes from a slab to walls in a day, it's like a magic trick. What's hard is I'm slower than the young lads and I second-guess my measurements. I sometimes ask one of those AI chat things on my phone to check my stair maths at night, when nobody's watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the real problems, like the price of houses and the fact that I'm still the only woman on the site. I'd probably post something on the women in trades group like, see, they still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can keep learning at my own pace and get my level two certificate before I'm sixty. I came into this late, so I've got a lot of catching up to do, and boring years would let me do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Larchfield, finish the college course on Thursdays, and keep the savings ticking over. Mo and I have about three months put by, and I'd want it nearer five before I think about stopping at sixty-four or so. Maybe I'd use the chat thing a bit more for revision, it's handy for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite pleased. Like the forecast says rain and it turns out sunny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check your stair maths with an AI tool at night. Why at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want the lads seeing me do it. They'd think I can't work out a rise and going, that's the height and depth of each step. I can, I just like to be sure before I cut an expensive stringer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would be most pleased with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernie, I think. He's sixty-one and he hates every new gadget head office sends. He'd be in the cabin saying, told you, kettle on.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's deal with the real problems like house prices and why I'm still the only woman on site. I'd post on the women in trades group that they still need us.
S0.think: Privately it means I can keep learning at my own pace and get my level two certificate before sixty. I came in late and boring years would let me catch up.
S0.do: Keeps working at Larchfield Homes and finishes the Thursday college course. Keeps saving to stretch three months of cover towards five, and uses an AI chat tool a little more for revision.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, like rain forecast and sunshine instead.
S0.quote: They'd think I can't work out a rise and going, that's the height and depth of each step.
S0.fieldNote: Vera is a late starter who's proud and a bit self-conscious about it. She already uses AI quietly, almost secretly, to check her work, which hints she's more comfortable with it than her public image. Her public line goes straight to fairness and women in the trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the changes should be negotiated, not dumped on us. The union got me into this trade, and they should be at the table when the factory makes more of the house and we do less on site. That's what I'd say at the meeting and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I've watched it happen already. Five years ago carpenters built those walls on site, and now a factory does it and we just bolt them up. Steady change means more of the house comes off the lorry finished, and fewer of us are needed to stand it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the union's training list early and look at moving into checking work, quality inspection, where you go round with a tablet and sign off that the panels are fixed right. I'd use the AI thing properly to study for it, instead of hiding it. And I'd keep putting fifty a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not lost. I changed careers once at fifty-four, so I know I can, I just didn't fancy doing it twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the factory does more and more. Do you know anyone who works in one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Danny's mate Kieran works at the panel factory over in the industrial park. He says it's mostly machines cutting and nailing, and he watches screens and fixes jams. He earns more than me, mind, and he's warm all winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mo say about you retraining again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh and say not another course, Vera. Then he'd make me a flask and drive me to it. He drives buses, so he knows about change, they've got all sorts of tracking on him now.

S1.say: I'd say the changes must be negotiated, not dumped on us. The union got me into this trade, so it should be at the table when factories make more of the house and we do less on site.
S1.think: Privately I've already watched it happen, with factory panels replacing on-site framing. Steady change means more of the house arrives finished and fewer of us are needed to stand it up.
S1.do: Gets onto the union training list early and aims for a quality inspection role signing off panel work. Uses the AI tool openly to study and keeps putting fifty a week into savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not lost, because she's changed careers once already, though she didn't want to do it twice.
S1.quote: Five years ago carpenters built those walls on site, and now a factory does it and we just bolt them up.
S1.fieldNote: She speaks from direct experience of factory-built panels, which makes her picture of steady change very concrete. She's willing to move into inspection and to drop her secrecy about AI. Her partner's support comes through warmly and matters to her confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income, and I'd say it loudly. If machines can do every job by 2028, then the wealth has to be shared, or we'll have riots. I'd be at the union rally and on the women in trades group asking who's going to look after the people who built these houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared stiff. I'd be sixty and out of work, and Mo would be too, because a bus that drives itself is the first thing they'd roll out. Three months of savings goes nowhere when both wages stop in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the car payment by handing it back, and we'd cancel the trip to see Ruth. I'd apply for every bit of help going and I'd go to the union, because that's where help comes from. I'd also ask Larchfield if there's any job at all supervising the robots, even nights, even sweeping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and angry at the same time. Mostly angry that we got no warning, so people like me can't plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bill would you stop paying first, if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, then the phone contracts, then my college course, which would break my heart a bit. I'd never miss the rent. My mum drilled that into me: roof first, then food, then the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about supervising the robots. Is that realistic for you, as a junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. They'd want someone younger who knows computers properly. But I'd ask anyway, because you don't get if you don't ask, and I've used that chat thing more than the lads have.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that this is the moment for a basic income. If machines do every job by 2028 the wealth must be shared, and I'd ask at union rallies who'll look after the people who built these houses.
S2.think: Privately I'd be scared stiff. I'd be sixty and out of work, Mo's bus driving would go too, and three months of savings goes nowhere when both wages stop.
S2.do: Hands back the car and cancels the trip to see Ruth, then applies for every bit of help and leans on the union. Asks Larchfield for any job supervising robots, even nights or sweeping up.
S2.feel: Frightened and angry, mostly angry that there was no warning to plan.
S2.quote: Roof first, then food, then the rest.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture hits her household twice, since her partner's job is just as exposed. She's realistic that a junior at sixty is unlikely to be picked for robot supervision, but she would still ask. Anger at the lack of warning sits right beside the fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to get a plan in place: retraining money, early pensions, a wage for people pushed out. I'd say it at the branch, and I'd probably stand for something at the women in trades group, which I've always said I'm too busy to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me sixty-three, and that's close to where Mo and I wanted to stop anyway. If I can get inspection work for a few years and save hard, we might just limp to the finish. It's tight, but it's a plan, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the inspection course this winter, not next year, and get the AI tools into my head properly since inspection's all tablets and reports. We'd put Mo's overtime straight into savings and aim for six months by 2030. And we'd look at whether one of us can take a small pension early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. I'm better when I've got a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand for something at the women in trades group. What's changed your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if five years is all we've got, the young women coming in need someone saying don't train for the bits the robot will do. I wish someone had told me that about cooking. I could be that nagging aunt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Danny, as an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the robots' wiring. Somebody has to fix them when they go wrong, and I'd rather it was my son than the company that sold them.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to get a plan in place: retraining money, early pensions and a wage for people pushed out. I'd finally stand for a role at the women in trades group.
S3.think: Privately sixty-three is close to when Mo and I wanted to stop anyway. With a few years of inspection work and hard saving, we might just limp to the finish.
S3.do: Starts the inspection course this winter and learns the AI tools properly, since inspection runs on tablets and reports. Puts Mo's overtime into savings, aiming for six months by 2030, and checks early pension options.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, steadier once she has a list.
S3.quote: It's tight, but it's a plan, not a cliff.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns the panic of the fast picture into a plan she can manage. She moves straight to mentoring younger women, which seems to give her purpose as well as worry. She now treats AI as a tool to learn openly rather than something to hide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, so let's not waste it. Every apprentice starting now should be told the truth, and the government should be paying for second careers, not leaving it to luck like mine was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's almost a happy ending. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, on my allotment, and I'd have had ten good years in a trade I love. My worry is for the young women I've been nagging, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Larchfield and get my certificate, then do inspection in my last few years if my knees give up. I'd keep saving the normal amount. And I'd put real hours into the women in trades mentoring, maybe two evenings a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, and a bit proud that I'd made it. A small worry for the girls coming up behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your last day on site look like, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernie would be long gone by then, so some young foreman would give me a cake from the garage. I'd walk round the last house and touch the frame, daft as it sounds. Then I'd go home and Mo would have the kettle on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you weren't sure about changing careers twice. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. With ten years I don't have to change twice, I just have to finish once. That's the difference, really.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, so don't waste it. Apprentices should be told the truth, and the government should fund second careers instead of leaving it to luck.
S4.think: Privately it's almost a happy ending: sixty-eight, retired on my allotment after ten good years in a trade I love. My worry is for the young women I mentor.
S4.do: Keeps working at Larchfield, finishes her certificate and moves into inspection later if her knees give out. Saves at the usual rate and gives two evenings a month to mentoring women in trades.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit proud, with a small worry for the young women behind her.
S4.quote: With ten years I don't have to change twice, I just have to finish once.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets her retire on her own terms before the end point arrives, so her mood settles. Her concern shifts outward to the women she mentors. She put the whole difference between the timelines into one clear sentence.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Two years and both Mo and me out at once. What would help is a proper income for people who lose work, paid for by the companies making the robots, and being able to take a pension at sixty without losing half of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women. Every time work changes, we get pushed out first and let back in last. I fought my way onto that site at fifty-four, and I'd hate the robots to be the thing that pushes me back off it.

headlineQuote: Every time work changes, we get pushed out first and let back in last.
portrait: Vera is a fifty-eight-year-old former care-home cook who joined a women-into-trades scheme at fifty-four and now works as an improver standing up factory-made timber-frame houses. She's a union-minded progressive who quietly uses AI to check her stair maths and would study for an inspection role if work shifted. Steady change leaves her uneasy because she has already seen factories take on-site framing. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because it ends her job and her partner's bus driving at once, while five years gives her a plan and ten years lets her finish her career on her own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because both she and Mo would lose their incomes in the same year with only three months saved.
whatWouldHelp: An income for people who lose work, paid for by the companies making the robots, and a pension at sixty without a big cut.
